scope: A verified annotated bibliography for the force fleet: SIPRI's 2024 military-expenditure and arms-transfer fact sheets; MP-IDSA and ORF defence-budget and procurement analyses by Laxman Kumar Behera; PRS Demand for Grants analyses for Defence and Home Affairs 2025-26 and PRS's 2017 police-reform report; the Common Cause–CSDS Status of Policing in India reports (2018, 2019, 2023, 2025); the Prakash Singh judgment; the Standing Committee reports as transcribed by PRS; the Agnipath debate papers on both sides; the CAG single-vendor finding; the comparative police-strength literature; and the court records and journalism of record for Bofors, Rafale, AgustaWestland, Tatra, Adarsh and Pegasus. Each document carries a two-sentence summary of what it establishes and what it does not. The file calibrates fifteen narratives the other seven domains will rate and sets base rates (police per lakh against the unverified 222 benchmark; defence share of GDP against the SIPRI peer set; pension share; CAPF vacancy; single-vendor share). It leaves out: the budget series themselves (union-defence, union-home and state-police domains write those rows; this file carries no series rows to avoid key collisions), footprint, procurement awards, and any claim about a person. Reachability: bprd.nic.in and cag.gov.in were unreachable (connection failed); pib.gov.in, factly.in, Wiley, Taylor & Francis and MIT Press returned 403 to the fetcher; Takshashila and CPR searches returned no police-reform results; CHRI's compliance page and the Sukna Wikipedia page returned 404. Wikipedia pages were used as summaries of court and press records for the cases (tier reported) where the primary order was not opened.

entities.label: SIPRI — Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2024
entities.sub: SIPRI Fact Sheet, April 2025 (Liang, Tian, Lopes da Silva, Scarazzato, Karim, Guiberteau Ricard)
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes: India was the fifth-largest military spender in 2024 at US$86.1 billion, up 1.6% in real terms from 2023 and 42% from 2015, equal to 2.3% of GDP (2.5% in 2015) and 3.2% of world spending; world total US$2,718 billion, 2.5% of world GDP; table 1 gives China [314] (1.7% GDP), USA 997 (3.4%), Russia [149] (7.1%), Saudi Arabia [80.3] (7.3%), UK 81.8 (2.3%), Pakistan not in top 15 [documented]

The fact sheet notes India's policy earmarking 75% of capital outlays (≈22% of total military spending) for domestic procurement, with continued import reliance for combat aircraft [documented]

entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes (from BPR&D and NCRB as of January 2016): sanctioned strength 181 police per lakh, actual 137, vacancies 24% (about 5.5 lakh); 86% of state police are constabulary; police spending about 3% of central and state budgets combined; only 14% of Modernisation of Police Forces funds used by states in 2015-16; IPC conviction rate 47% in 2015; it states a "United Nations recommended standard of 222 police per lakh" [reported]

entities.label: "UN-recommended 222 police per lakh" (benchmark of uncertain provenance)
entities.sub: A ratio repeated in Indian policy writing (PRS 2017, Standing Committee and press) and attributed to the United Nations
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.

d: Establishes: seven directives — a State Security Commission; DGP selection from a UPSC-empanelled list of three senior-most officers with a minimum two-year tenure; two-year minimum tenure for IG, DIG, SP and SHO; separation of investigation from law and order (first in towns above 10 lakh); a Police Establishment Board for transfers below DSP; Police Complaints Authorities at state (retired HC/SC judge) and district (retired district judge) level; a National Security Commission to select CAPF chiefs with two-year tenure [documented]

entities.label: ORF — The Case for Agnipath (Behera & Kaushal, 2023)
entities.sub: ORF Issue Brief No. 567, 16 August 2023 (updated from 2022), Laxman Kumar Behera and Vinay Kaushal — an independent proponents' economic case (not a government document)
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes: defence pension rose 163% from ₹45,500 crore (2013-14) to ₹1,19,696 crore (2022-23 BE) while total MoD spending rose 107%; pay & allowances plus pension ₹2,87,040 crore = 79% of MoD revenue expenditure in 2022-23 (BE); military pensioners 3.8 lakh (1950), 6 lakh (1970), 26.8 lakh military veterans or dependents plus 6.1 lakh defence civilians, 32.9 lakh in all (2021-04-01); an Agniveer's composite pay ₹30,000 (year 1) to ₹40,000 (year 4) a month, ₹45,338 average including the government's 30% Seva Nidhi contribution, against ₹59,976 for a regular soldier — ₹1,75,656 less a year; first-year saving ₹1,054 crore on an assumed 60,000 recruits; the authors state "there will be no savings in the near to medium term" and pension savings arrive only after 2044, when 34% (4,54,688 of 13.3 lakh other ranks) would be pensionable; MoD projects average age falling from 32 to 24–26 [reported]

Does not establish: operational effects — the brief concedes teething problems, infrastructure costs for larger training cohorts, and that the officer cadre is "equally ripe for reform"; it is an argument for the scheme, written by its best-known defender [analytic]

entities.label: DPG — The Agnipath Scheme: Analysis and A Way Forward (Hooda, 2022)
entities.sub: Delhi Policy Group policy brief, 24 June 2022, Lt Gen Deependra Singh Hooda (retd), former Northern Army Commander — the critics' case
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes the stated objections: shortened training for soldiers "straight away pitched into situations on a live border"; dilution of unit cohesion with "two classes of soldiers with different service conditions"; tension between all-India recruitment and the regimental system; the 25% retention competition; loss of institutional experience; the social question of releasing 75% at 21–25 without pension or gratuity; recommends treating the first four years as a validation period [reported]

Does not establish: costs — the brief offers no counter-estimate to the ORF savings arithmetic; both sides agree the pension bill is the driver and differ on whether the operational risk is worth it [analytic]

Document trail: Bofors — Swedish Radio 16 Apr 1987 and The Hindu's document series 1987–89; Rafale — The Hindu 2019 (the MoD note of 2015-11-24, The Hindu 8 Feb 2019, not opened here). Payment / process: Bofors — documented payments to agents traced to Swiss accounts (a payment, not a process anomaly); Rafale — a process anomaly (the MoD dissent note), with no documented payment to an Indian official. No conviction of any Indian public servant in either.

narratives.claim: Rafale was a scam: the price was inflated (this entry); the companion claim that Reliance was chosen as offset partner at the Indian government's behest is narrative 15.
narratives.strongestCase: A 36-aircraft purchase replaced a 126-aircraft tender in April 2015; opposition figures put the per-aircraft price at ₹1,570 crore against ₹526 crore; Mediapart (November 2021, via Newslaundry) published invoices it says show at least €7.5 million in secret commissions from Dassault to a middleman's company in 2007–12, reported that he held MoD documents on the negotiators' price calculations, and said the CBI and ED had the evidence from October 2018 and did not act [reported; Dassault and the MoD deny corruption]; the 2018 SC judgment relied on a statement that pricing had been examined by the CAG and the PAC, which the government later sought to correct (literature:c005); a French judicial investigation into suspected corruption, influence peddling and favouritism has been open since June 2021, and a French ambassador's note of 2023-07-25 complained of Indian delays on criminal cooperation in general.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Supreme Court (2018-12-14; review 2019-11-14) found the process broadly followed and declined to compare prices ("it is certainly not the job of this Court to carry out a comparison of the pricing details"); the CAG (Report No. 3 of 2019, not opened) reported the IGA 2.86% below the audit-aligned price; ministers claimed a saving of 9% (basic aircraft, Jaitley) to 20% (package, Jaitley/Akbar), never contradicted by a court or audit opened here; the Mediapart payment dates (2007–12) fall mostly in the UPA era and precede the 36-aircraft IGA; no court or audit has found corruption.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a finding by the French investigating judge of payments to Indian decision-makers, or the CAG report (unopened) showing the IGA dearer than the escalated bid. Down to debunked: the French probe closes with no finding.

Para 5 appears to be an over reaction" (file noting of 2016-01-11, published in February 2019); the head of the Indian Negotiating Team, Air Marshal S.B.P. Sinha, said "No such objections were ever brought to me by anybody from the Ministry of Defence" (ThePrint); the SC dismissed the review on 2019-11-14 ("All aspects were considered by the competent authority"); an internal dissent note is evidence of debate, not of wrongdoing.

narratives.claim: Bofors was buried: the Congress governments protected the recipients of the kickbacks.
narratives.strongestCase: Agent payments are documented in Swiss accounts; The Hindu stopped publishing Bofors stories 'under immense government pressure' (Wikipedia, single-sourced to The Hoot) [reported, single source]; the Italian agent left India in 1993 and extradition from Malaysia and later Argentina failed, India not appealing the Argentine ruling in 2007 (The Federal); in December 2005 the Union's law officer told the Crown Prosecutor there was no case, the London accounts (€3 million and $1 million) were de-frozen and about ₹210 million withdrawn; the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, allowing the withdrawal, said "there are certain malafide intentions in the case" (Wikipedia); the CBI sought withdrawal against the Italian agent and the Delhi court allowed closure on 2011-03-04; the case ended without any conviction after 39 years.
narratives.strongestCounter: Delhi HC (2004-02-04, Kapoor J) held after 13 years of CBI investigation that "the public servants are completely absolved of all the allegations" (para 140), while directing cheating charges against the Hindujas (para 141(ii)); the line that the late Prime Minister is 'entitled to be seen as innocent' is a quotation from Rajiv Gandhi Ekta Samiti v UOI; the Swedish police chief who leaked the documents said in 2012 that Rajiv Gandhi had done nothing wrong; the Hindujas were discharged in 2005; the CBI's own SLP was dismissed in 2018 for a 4,522-day delay; non-Congress governments held the file too — V.P. Singh 1989–90, Chandra Shekhar 1990–91 (Congress-supported), NDA 1998–2004 (which filed the first chargesheet in 1999) and 2014–26 — and none secured a conviction.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a recipient-side bank record naming an Indian public servant. The former 'Down' trigger has resolved without moving the narrative: the 2026-08-06 order dismissed a private appeal (Ajay K Agrawal) after refusing an adjournment and decided nothing on the merits (HT, The Federal).

narratives.claim: The Indian government used Pegasus on opposition politicians, journalists, activists and Supreme Court staff (including an old number once registered to a judge).
narratives.strongestCase: About 300 Indian numbers on the leaked NSO client-interest list, including "senior journalists, doctors, political persons, and even some Court staff" (SC order, 2021-10-27, para 6); Amnesty forensics found infections on some Indian phones; the Union filed only an omnibus denial and declined a detailed affidavit; the SC committee found malware on 5 of 29 devices and recorded that the government did not cooperate; NSO says it sells only to governments; the Union has never stated whether any agency acquired Pegasus.
narratives.strongestCounter: The committee could not establish that the malware was Pegasus or who deployed it; the IT Minister told Parliament on 2021-07-19 that a number on a list is not evidence of use; MoD told the Rajya Sabha on 2021-08-09 it "has not had any transaction with NSO Group Technologies" — this covers MoD only, not MHA or the intelligence agencies; the list also included BJP ministers (Ashwini Vaishnaw, Prahlad Patel), so it cut across parties; Justice Arun Mishra said the listed number had not been his since 2013-14; on 2025-04-29 the SC (Surya Kant and Kotiswar Singh JJ) said there is nothing wrong with a country possessing spyware for security and the question is against whom it is used, that the technical report will not be made public, and that individuals may be told whether their own devices were examined; the matter was adjourned to 2025-07-30 (later hearings not opened).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: individual disclosures to petitioners under the 2025 direction attributing an infection to an Indian agency, or a contract record for an Indian agency. Down: a forensic attribution of the five infections to a non-state or foreign actor.

narratives.claim: AgustaWestland bribes reached senior UPA-era officials, a Congress party office-holder and the Air Force leadership (popularly: 'the top of the UPA government').
narratives.strongestCase: A middleman's note presented in the Italian court lists Manmohan Singh and others as advisors 'to target' and allocates bribes as "AF" €6 million, "BUR" €8.4 million, "Pol" €6 million and "AP" €3 million; Italian prosecutors alleged that Ahmed Patel received kickbacks (the middleman told the Italian court he did not know who 'AP' was); the CBI's 2017-09-01 chargesheet alleges that the former IAF chief conspired to cut the service ceiling from 6,000 m to 4,500 m [alleged]; Defence Minister A.K. Antony said in March 2013, "Yes, corruption has taken place in the helicopter deal and bribes have been taken"; Italy arrested the supplier's CEO; India cancelled the contract for integrity-pact breach and encashed ₹2,068 crore of guarantees; the CBI arrested the former IAF chief and extradited the middleman.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Busto Arsizio court (October 2014) acquitted the Finmeccanica and AgustaWestland heads of international corruption and convicted them only of false invoicing; the former IAF chief was not tried in Italy; the Italian courts acquitted the executives at final instance (2018, upheld 2019) and the consultant Haschke was acquitted on appeal in Brescia (2025-06-30); the Indian trial had not commenced as of the SC's February 2025 bail order (FIR 2013-03-13); denials on record: the UPA government's 'nothing to hide' (2013), the middleman's 'never met any Gandhi', and documents showing the specification change was agreed by several agencies including the PMO and the SPG.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a conviction in the Delhi CBI court. Down: acquittal or discharge of the Indian accused.

narratives.claim: India under-spends on defence; it should spend 3% of GDP.
narratives.strongestCase: The Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommended about 3%; PRS puts 2025-26 at 1.9% of GDP (about 1.5% without pensions), 13% of Union expenditure against 17% in 2014-15; capital outlay below 30% of the budget every year 2014-15 to 2024-25; the Ministry received ₹9.01 lakh crore for capital outlay in 2021-26 against a plan projection of ₹17.46 lakh crore (48% shortfall) and highlighted (as recorded by PRS from the 15th Finance Commission report) that consistent shortfalls had led to 'serious capability gaps'; peers above 3% exist — USA 3.4%, and Pakistan (2.7%) and South Korea (2.6%) are above India's 2.3% (SIPRI 2024 table 1).
narratives.strongestCounter: SIPRI puts India fifth in the world at US$86.1 billion, 2.3% of GDP — the median of the fifteen largest spenders (our computation from SIPRI table 1) and below the 2.5% global military burden (world spending / world GDP); SIPRI's country averages are 1.9% for countries not in conflict and 4.4% for countries in conflict; the MoD itself said 3% of GDP (₹10.7 lakh crore, 21% of central spending in 2025-26) would produce allocations the services may not be able to absorb (PRS); PRS notes capital allocations have improved in recent years; the services' projections are demands.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: This is a value question about the definition: PRS's 1.9% (about 1.5% without pension) is the MoD budget; SIPRI's 2.3% includes paramilitary forces. UPA control: capital outlay was 32% of the defence budget in 2013-14 and SIPRI had India at 2.5% in 2015, so the gap to 3% predates 2014. The Ministry already claims capability gaps, so the deciding test is an independent CAG or SC capability audit, not a first claim of a gap.

narratives.claim: The defence budget is eaten by pensions and pay, leaving nothing for modernisation.
narratives.strongestCase: Pensions 24% and salaries 26% of the MoD's 2025-26 allocation (PRS's 'salaries' line includes civilians, R&D and civil-estimate salaries); pay & allowances plus pension 79% of MoD revenue expenditure in 2022-23 (a share of revenue expenditure, not of the total demand); pension +163% 2013-14 → 2022-23 against +107% for the ministry; pension grew 11% a year against 9% for the total, 2013-14 → 2025-26 (PRS); capital outlay below 30% every year 2014-15 to 2024-25. [reported: PRS/ORF transcription of budget documents]
narratives.strongestCounter: Pensions are contracts with about 32.9 lakh pensioners (26.8 lakh military veterans or dependents and 6.1 lakh defence civilians, ORF, as of 2021-04-01) and rose by policy (OROP 2015, 7th CPC 2016); 'leaving nothing for modernisation' is contradicted by PRS Table 2: capital outlay ₹1,92,388 crore = 28% of the 2025-26 BE, up 13% over 2024-25 RE, and PRS says 'Allocation for capital acquisition has improved in recent years'; UPA-II baseline: capital was 32% of the defence budget in 2013-14; 'eaten' presumes modernisation is the only legitimate use of a force budget. Status: the pay-and-pension half is supported; the 'nothing for modernisation' half is not.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Down: a demand PDF showing the pension line falling as a share after Agnipath cohorts mature (not before 2044 by ORF's arithmetic). Upgrade of the figures to documented once the pay-pensions domain reproduces them from the Defence Pensions and Defence Services demand PDFs.

narratives.claim: Agnipath is a cost-cutting measure disguised as military reform.
narratives.strongestCase: Independent proponents (ORF Issue Brief 567) state there is "a strong financial imperative" and compute the saving; the 75% released get no pension; without such reform, they say, the budget "would have become unsustainable"; DPG (Hooda): "The government and the military are silent on the issue of manpower savings ... it is apparent that the rising pay and pension budget has been a key factor"; the PBOR scheme was mooted in 2020-21 under CDS Bipin Rawat amid concern over pensions (The Wire). Against this, ORF itself records that 'the government denied any financial motive' (Rajnath Singh: "We never see the army from the point of view of savings"), and the DMA said pension savings were 'most definitely' not a consideration.
narratives.strongestCounter: The reform aim is real (MoD's goal of cutting average age from 32 to 24–26); ORF finds no pension savings before 2044, so the near-term rationale is youth profile, not cost; the critics (DPG) contest operational risk. Status: the cost motive is well supported as a co-driver, the 'disguised' framing is partly supported (the official denial exists), and a 'merely cost-cutting' reading is unsupported.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: an MoD or DMA document (cabinet note, DMA study, Standing Committee answer) that names pension savings as an objective. Down: evidence that the 2020–21 proposal under CDS Bipin Rawat was framed only on youth profile. (The earlier trigger — MoD disavowing the fiscal rationale — already happened in June 2022.)

narratives.claim: India is dangerously under-policed: the UN recommends 222 police per lakh and India has 155.
narratives.strongestCase: BPR&D (via PRS) gives 155 per lakh on 2023-01-01, Bihar 81; the states fill only about 77% of sanctioned posts (SPIR 2019); PRS 2017 calls 222 the 'United Nations recommended standard' and the Standing Committee repeats it. Note: 155 (2023, PRS 2025) and 222 (PRS 2017) come from different documents; PRS 2025 does not mention 222.
narratives.strongestCounter: 222 is attributed to the UN by PRS 2017, whose footnotes ([8], [33]) point to BPR&D documents (DoPO 2016 and 'National Requirement of Manpower for 8-hour Shifts', Aug 2014), not a UN document; no UN instrument was located; Africa Check (2019) reports that 'The UN did not respond to our queries about if they have any ratio' and traces the often-cited 1:450 ratio to US policing of occupied Germany in 1945; the shortfall against India's own sanctioned ratio in force (196.23 on 2022-01-01, MHA) is the documented one — about 21%; 20 of 36 states/UTs are below 222, including every large state except Punjab, in BJP-run and opposition-run states alike (PRS Table 15); the Union fills its own forces to about 90.5%. 'Dangerously' is a normative word no source opened evidences.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a UN document that sets 222. Down to debunked: a UN statement that no such norm exists (the UN declined to answer Africa Check in 2019). Optional upgrade for 155: the 2021 Rajya Sabha unstarred answer or BPR&D DoPO 2023 opened directly.

narratives.claim: No state fully complies with the Supreme Court's 2006 Prakash Singh directives; most constituted SSCs and PEBs on paper in diluted form, and substantive compliance is rare.
narratives.strongestCase: SPIR 2018 calls compliance "a story of a monumental non-compliance"; CHRI (Sept 2021) finds 27 of 28 states have constituted an SSC by Police Act or government order but that states "rejected, ignored, or diluted significant features of the directives"; PRS 2017 documents ministerial use of police and recommends statutory limits; SPIR 2019 finds 12% of SSP/DIG-rank officers transferred within two years in 2016, higher in election years.
narratives.strongestCounter: Several states passed Police Acts after 2006; SPIR 2019: premature transfers of SSPs and DIGs fell "from 37 percent in 2007 to 13 percent in 2016" and the judgment "appears to have a tangible impact"; the Union formed the National Security Commission in 2017 (SPIR 2018). Response: CHRI records the states' route as enacting their own Police Acts or orders that dilute the directives; no state's comment was sought for this file. Data run to 2016–17 (SPIR) and 2021 (CHRI).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The compliance table now exists (CHRI 2021); what would move this is the SC's compliance affidavits or the Justice K.T. Thomas Committee report (2010) opened, or a post-2021 state-by-state reassessment.

narratives.claim: Custodial torture is routine and the police themselves justify it.
narratives.strongestCase: Police personnel themselves justify coercion — well supported as an attitude rate (single survey, reported): SPIR 2025 (8,276 state/Delhi police, 82 locations, 16 states + Delhi, Nov 2023 – Jan 2024; CAPFs not covered) finds 30% justify third-degree against the accused in serious criminal cases (9% in petty offences, 9% against uncooperative witnesses); 30% have a high and 32% a moderate propensity to justify torture; 64% justify third-degree in a kidnapped-minor scenario (19% absolutely, 45% sometimes); 11% say hitting an absconding accused's family is absolutely justified and 30% sometimes; 30% would bar lawyers from interrogation. State spread: Gujarat and Jharkhand highest on the propensity index, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh high, Kerala lowest (party is text only). NCRB counting gaps documented in SPIR 2025 chapter 8. Separately, half of 15,562 CITIZENS condone violence on criminals in police custody (SPIR 2018) — a public attitude, not police.
narratives.strongestCounter: 'Routine' is an incidence claim and is contested: the closest incidence-like item (Table 5.8, police perception of IO practice on third-degree in serious offences) is 11% many times, 16% sometimes, 14% once or twice, 52% never; NCRB recorded 76 custodial deaths in 2020 against NCAT's 111, of which NCAT attributes 51 to torture; none of this is a measured incidence rate. 71–79% of police rate torture-prevention, human-rights and evidence-based-interrogation training as very important; answers are to hypotheticals; India has not ratified the Convention Against Torture. Denial: none found; MHA and state police were not asked.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: State-wise custodial deaths per lakh officers (NCRB, Parliament answers) joined by the state-police domain would turn an attitude rate into an outcome rate.

narratives.claim: Defence procurement is rigged through single-vendor tenders.
narratives.strongestCase: CAG Report No. 4 of 2007 (Army and Ordnance Factories, pp. 10-11, via ORF) found 60% of audited Indian Army procurement cases ended with a single vendor qualified (Army single-vendor prevalence reported; report unopened); CAG Report No. 3 of 2019 (Capital Acquisition in IAF, pp. 31-32, as quoted by ORF) found QRs 'vendor-driven, and subject to repeated changes during the procurement process' with 'unwarranted specifications' [reported]; DAP 2020 still provides for ab-initio single-vendor and IGA/FMS routes without offsets; the fleet's CPPP slice shows services' headquarters buying with 40%+ single bids.
narratives.strongestCounter: The CAG attributed single-vendor outcomes to QR drafting; neither audit as quoted names a beneficiary; much defence equipment has one or two makers worldwide; the works branch (79% of the security slice) single-bids at 0.1%; "rigged" requires a beneficiary and a mechanism that no audit opened here names.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a later CAG compendium (unopened; cag.gov.in blocked) tying single-vendor cases to specific vendors and officials. Down: a current single-vendor rate near commercial norms. Open CAG 4/2007 and 3/2019, including the MoD replies printed in them, to record the denial; if confirmed, the prevalence component can move to documented.

narratives.claim: India is the world's largest arms importer, proving Make in India has failed.
narratives.strongestCase: SIPRI ranks India second (behind wartime Ukraine) with 8.3% of global imports 2020–24 and 8.2% in 2021–25; SIPRI 2026: 'India's recent orders or planned orders—including up to 140 combat aircraft from France and 6 submarines from Germany—indicate its continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers'.
narratives.strongestCounter: The premise 'world's largest' is false for 2020–24 and 2021–25 (second, behind Ukraine). Imports fell 9.3% (2015–19 → 2020–24) and 4.0% (2016–20 → 2021–25); Russia's share fell from 70% (2011–15) to 51% (2016–20) and 40% (2021–25); SIPRI attributes part of the fall to growing domestic design and production; deliveries in 2020–24 reflect contracts signed before or around 2014 (delivery lag); whether India also ranked first under UPA-II (SIPRI 2010–14) is not opened here; rank follows size. The government's own production and export releases are a self-reported counter-position, not opened here.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The SIPRI 2021–25 test has resolved: imports did not rise (−4.0%), but SIPRI flags reliance as likely to increase. Next test: SIPRI 2022–26 together with the MoD's domestic-procurement share of capital acquisition. Status stays contested for the inference.

narratives.claim: Adarsh: officials, politicians and military officers irregularly obtained flats on government land (supported by the commission, the CAG and the HC); the land was meant for Kargil widows (disputed: rejected by the commission's interim report).
narratives.strongestCase: A state judicial commission (final report April 2013) indicted four former Chief Ministers, two ministers and 12 bureaucrats, found 25 illegal allotments including 22 benami, and found 25 of the society's 102 members ineligible; the CAG (2011, as quoted by Wikipedia) found that "a group of select officials, placed in key posts, could subvert rules and regulations in order to grab prime government land"; CBI arrested two retired Major Generals and others in 2012; Bombay HC ordered demolition in 2016.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Patil Commission's own interim report (April 2012) found the land belonged to Maharashtra and was not reserved for Kargil war widows; Sushilkumar Shinde said the same on affidavit (May 2011) and denied receiving favours; the MoD claimed the land in 2012 and ownership was never finally adjudicated; the state cabinet rejected the report in December 2013 and then partly accepted it days later (departmental inquiry against 12 officials) after Rahul and Sonia Gandhi objected; the HC quashed the sanction to prosecute Ashok Chavan (2017); the SC on 2016-07-22 directed the Centre to take possession and not demolish pending appeal; no final verdict as of 2024 (ThePrint; 2025-26 status not checked) — and no-conviction status is the base rate for such cases, so it does not discriminate. Symmetry: all those indicted are Congress/NCP politicians or officials; Ashok Chavan joined the BJP in February 2024.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A CBI court verdict either way; a final civil ruling on MoD vs State ownership of the plot; the SC's final decision on the demolition appeal.

narratives.claim: Tatra: the Army bought about 7,000 Tatra trucks over more than two decades through BEML via Vectra-group intermediaries at allegedly inflated prices (an allegation, not a finding against BEML).
narratives.strongestCase: The then Army chief said in 2012 he was offered ₹14 crore to clear a tranche of 'sub-standard' trucks; about 7,000 trucks were bought over more than two decades through a single public-sector channel, and the alleged pricing chain ran through Vectra-group entities before BEML (Wikipedia); the bribe-offer case is on trial (charges framed 2019-08-02, upheld by the Delhi HC in July 2022; former Defence Minister Antony cross-examined as a prosecution witness in 2022).
narratives.strongestCounter: The CBI closed its procurement inquiry in 2014 for insufficient evidence to file a chargesheet; a bribe offer alleged by the buyer's own chief is evidence the offer was refused, not that prior purchases were corrupt; no pricing audit was opened. BEML's 2012 rebuttal and the special court's later handling of the closure report are not opened here.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Opening the CBI closure report and the special court's order on it, and the Defence Minister's 2012 statement to Parliament.

narratives.claim: Anil Ambani's Reliance Group (Reliance Defence Ltd / Reliance Aerostructure Ltd; JV Dassault Reliance Aerospace Ltd) was chosen as Dassault's offset partner for the 36-Rafale deal at the Indian government's behest.
narratives.strongestCase: Former French President François Hollande (in office May 2012–May 2017, so on the other side of the 2015 joint statement and the 2016 IGA) told Mediapart (2018-09-21): "We didn't have any say in this matter. It is the Indian government which had proposed this service group, and Dassault who negotiated with Ambani. We didn't have the choice, we took the interlocutor who was given to us"; his office said he stood by the remarks (ET, citing NDTV). Asked by AFP in Montreal the next day, he repeated that the name of Reliance Group had appeared as part of a 'new formula' in the negotiations, decided by the Modi government after it came to power, and that France "did not choose Reliance in any way" (Scroll, quoting AFP via Le Monde; AFP) — Scroll's point is that he did not deny his remarks. Mediapart (October 2018, as reproduced and translated by The Wire, 2018-10-10) reported an internal Dassault document recording that deputy CEO Loïk Segalen, presenting the Nagpur JV to staff representatives on 2017-05-11, said it was "impératif et obligatoire" for Dassault to accept this "contrepartie" to obtain the Rafale India export contract; Dassault's reply is in the counter. Reliance Aerostructure Ltd came into being only on 2015-04-24, after the 2015-04-10 joint statement (the petitioners' point, recorded in the SC order). A French judge was appointed in June 2021 to lead a judicial investigation into alleged corruption and favouritism in the deal (Wikipedia).
narratives.strongestCounter: Every other party denies it, on the record and when asked. The Indian MoD (2018-09-21): "neither the government nor the French government had any say in the commercial decision" (ET; AFP). The French Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs communiqué (2018-09-21): "The French government is in no manner involved in the choice of Indian industrial partners", French companies having 'full freedom' to choose them (ET; Wikipedia). Dassault's press release (2018-09-21) says it decided on the Reliance partnership under DPP and Make in India and has partnered several Indian firms (ET); its October 2018 reply to Mediapart says it "freely chose" Reliance and that Segalen was informing the Central Works Council, as French rules require, of the DRAL JV created "to fulfil some of the offsets commitments" (The Wire); Le Monde's Julien Bouissou read the Segalen note as a labour-law disclosure about an offset plant built outside France, and an industry observer told The Wire the 'trade-off' would be argued to mean offsets in general, not Reliance in particular. Hollande did not walk back his account, but he separated 'proposed' from 'compelled': asked by AFP whether India had pressured Dassault, he said he was 'unaware' and that 'only Dassault can comment' (Scroll; AFP). The SC (2018-12-14) found no "substantial material on record to show that this is a case of commercial favouritism", the choice of IOP resting with the vendor under DPP 2013, and recorded a "categorical denial, from every side" of the Hollande interview. The February 2012 Dassault pact the SC noted was with Reliance Industries (Mukesh Ambani; 'another business group' per the SC), not the Anil Ambani group that formed the JV — the SC's 'parent Reliance company' (para 32) conflates the two, so the 2012 pact does not by itself count against the claim; NDTV, citing Dassault sources, reported that talks moved to Anil Ambani's Reliance Defence at Aero India in February 2015 because the defence business passed from Mukesh to Anil and the firm had land near a runway (via Wikipedia). Credibility context: Hollande made the remark when Mediapart asked him about Reliance Entertainment's funding of a film produced by his partner Julie Gayet (Mediapart); Reliance Entertainment called the reports 'baseless allegations', said it signed no agreement with Gayet or her company and made no payment to either, and participated only through a French financing partner (Livemint, 2018-09-26). The IAF deputy chief (Air Marshal Nambiar, Sept 2018) said Dassault's own share of the ₹30,000 crore offsets was about ₹6,500 crore, so no single partner could receive ₹30,000 crore. Evidence tier: alleged — named parties (Hollande, Mediapart, the petitioners) assert it, the denials above are its contra, and no document shows the Indian side named Reliance.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a French judicial finding, or a document showing the Indian side named Reliance. Down: the French investigation closes without a favouritism finding; or the Segalen document is shown to be misreported or about something else (e.g. offsets in general rather than the Reliance JV).

narratives.claim: Many Indian police personnel say they justify third-degree methods against suspects: in a 2023–24 survey of 8,276 state and Delhi police personnel in 16 states and Delhi, about 30% said third-degree methods are justified against the accused in serious cases.
narratives.strongestCase: SPIR 2025 (8,276 police personnel of 16 state forces and Delhi Police at 82 locations; fieldwork November 2023–January 2024; report launched 2025-03-26): 30% justify third-degree methods against the accused in serious criminal cases (9% in petty offences); 64% in a kidnapped-minor scenario (19% absolutely, 45% somewhat); 30% have a high and 32% a moderate propensity to justify torture; the report finds the cumulative responses in support of torture higher than those rejecting it on each necessity question. The headline figure is in the Common Cause executive summary and ran on the PTI wire (National Herald, 2025-03-26). An earlier survey by the same team with a different instrument points the same way: SPIR 2019 (11,834 police personnel, 21 states) found "Four out of five personnel believe that there is nothing wrong in the police beating up criminals to extract confessions" — the same team, so not independent confirmation.
narratives.strongestCounter: A single survey of attitudes to hypotheticals, not incidence; 'third-degree' was not defined to respondents; the report flags social-desirability bias (which would push the true figure up, not down); majorities rate torture-prevention (71%) and human-rights (79%) training as very important. It is a convenience sample (SPIR 2025 Appendix 2, Stage 3: "Convenience sampling method was used") with equal quotas of about 400–500 interviews per state rather than shares proportional to force size, and 59% of respondents are of constabulary rank (Table A2.4), so 30% is a share of this sample, not a national estimate. CAPFs and the other states/UTs are not covered, and no UPA-era baseline exists. No response from MHA, BPR&D or any state police was found; none was asked. Evidence tier: reported — one NGO/academic survey with published instruments; the wire and LiveLaw coverage repeat it and add no independent confirmation.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A probability-sampled survey (e.g. by BPR&D or an independent pollster) with a defined instrument, or a second independent survey with a different instrument.

symmetryCheck: Cases: Bofors (Congress era) beside Rafale (BJP era) with identical fields — document trail (Swedish Radio/The Hindu 1987; The Hindu 2019), court record (Delhi HC 2004: no evidence any public servant received a bribe; SC 2018: no reason to intervene, review dismissed 2019), audit (JPC 1988 not opened; CAG 2019 not opened), foreign probe (Swiss documents obtained by letters rogatory 1990–2000; French PNF 2021–), Indian criminal case (Bofors yes, FIR 1990; Rafale no), outcome (no conviction in either). The agent-payment field is filled the same way for both: Bofors agent payments in Swiss accounts (1980s, Congress era) and the Mediapart-reported Dassault commissions of 2007–12 (mostly UPA era, before the 36-aircraft IGA). The lens produces the same shape for both governments: documented process anomalies, documented agent-side or dissent-side paper, and a judiciary that declined to find corruption. AgustaWestland beside Tatra (both exposed under A.K. Antony, both CBI cases from 2012–13; Tatra purchases spanned more than two decades and several governments): AgustaWestland has a dense record and no Indian verdict; Tatra has a bribe-offer trial pending and a procurement inquiry closed by the CBI in 2014 — neither has a verdict, and the depth difference is a finding about attention, not guilt. Pegasus: the UPA-II control does not apply (Pegasus postdates it), and the leaked list cut across parties. Literature: the principal budget analyst (Behera) wrote the IDSA series under both UPA and NDA and the ORF Agnipath brief under NDA; his adequacy measure (projection-vs-allocation gap) was 27% in UPA's last year and 25–30% in 2018–20, so the method does not flatter either side. The SPIR attitude series exists only for 2018–25, so no UPA baseline can be run; this is recorded as a void rather than inferred. States: this domain holds no state rows; the SPIR tables (reserved-post vacancies highest in UP and Haryana; premature transfers highest in Haryana and UP, both BJP-run in 2016; constabulary ratio met only in West Bengal and Bihar, opposition-run) are reported as printed and party is text only.
